title: Ajadapramātṛsiddhi — Proof of the Non-Insentient Subject
author: Utpaladeva
text:
The Ajadapramātṛsiddhi is the second member of Utpaladeva's Siddhitrayi — a trilogy of demonstrations in verse, composed in tenth-century Kashmir, in which each part secures one pillar of the recognition school by the ordinary means of proof. Where the first establishes the Lord, this work establishes the perceiver: the non-sentient-in-itself yet wholly aware subject without whom nothing could appear at all. Against realist and Buddhist accounts of cognition alike, it argues that objects are always encountered and never encounter; that what knows is not one item in the world's inventory; and that the insentient is such only as presented to awareness.

Its juice: if the knower cannot be found among the things it illuminates, the entire picture — world as object, self as one object among others — quietly inverts, and recognition becomes not a doctrine but the plain condition of having perceived anything whatsoever.
